title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: extended reality
concepts.definition: Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

defining_facts.text: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

The X in Extended Reality (XR) can be read as a variable, not only as part of 'extended', and its values such as A, V, and M denote augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR), while its many possible values form present or future immersive technologies.

Although adoption statistics can be misleading, earlier use forecasts discussed in the course indicate that extended reality, which covers augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR), has commercial potential in video games (about 34% or more than one third of applications), healthcare, engineering, live events, video entertainment, real estate, retail, and military (about 4% of application areas, a figure that may change); because worldwide military budgets are huge, even 4% is a large monetary amount, so penetration in the commercial space can be expected both percentage-wise and value-wise.

concepts.name: usability
concepts.definition: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user: the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

defining_facts.text: Usability is an explicit measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user.

The International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 standard defines usability as the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

The three crucial aspects of the International Standards Organization (ISO) 9241-210-2009 usability definition are that a usable product is intended for a specified group of users rather than everybody, that it supports a specified set of goals rather than every conceivable feature, and that it is designed for a specified context of use rather than all usage scenarios.

The three measures of usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction; effectiveness is whether the user can do what they want to do, efficiency is how fast the user can do what they want to do, and satisfaction is how satisfied the user is when using the system.

concepts.name: interaction design
concepts.definition: Interaction design is the activity of designing user input in an XR system from the user's point of view to make the user's interaction easy, effective, and seamless.

defining_facts.text: In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling, which relate to input and give the user ease of interacting with the system, and perceptual design and modeling, which relate to output and make the output appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived by the user, are both important for usability.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.

The design-prototype-evaluate loop includes the activities of interface design and interaction design, primarily designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view based on user requirements, while code design is a separate later design activity.

concepts.name: extended reality system
concepts.definition: An Extended reality system is an interactive system that comprises hardware, an XR engine as middleware, and the application layer, in which input devices track the user's actions and positions, send them as input data, the data is processed to render an environment, and output devices stimulate the user's senses.

defining_facts.text: Extended Reality (XR) systems are highly interactive like other interactive systems, and consideration of human factors is important to understand how easily a user can provide input and perceive output.
An Extended Reality (XR) system comprises hardware, the middleware that is the XR engine, and the application layer.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the user's actions and positions are tracked by input devices and sent as input data; the input data is processed and the environment is rendered; the XR engine, as middleware, uses hardware resources to generate output data; and output devices stimulate the user's senses with that output.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling of user input should follow a user-centered design approach so that the user can provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, perceptual design and modeling of output requires a user-centered design approach because it is crucial to ensure that generated output stimuli match the user's perception of them, so that the user can perceive and understand the output easily.

concepts.name: interactive system
concepts.definition: Interactive system is a system in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user, a lay person who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how it works.

defining_facts.text: Interactive computing systems, or interactive systems, are systems in which interaction takes place between the computer or system and the user.
In interactive systems, the user is a lay person or layman user who is not necessarily a technology expert and who wants to use the system rather than understand how the system works.
Designers of interactive systems that are intended to be used by laypersons should not force users to learn the underlying technology or understand the relevant technical terms.

concepts.name: user-centered design
concepts.definition: User-centered design (UCD) is a design approach in which users are actively or passively involved in the overall design lifecycle, and the design is based on the user's abilities, context, goals, needs, and expectations, ideally from the users' point of view rather than the programmer's convenience, to build a usable application.

defining_facts.text: The meaning of user-centric design varies by stakeholder, particularly by designer role: for a user interface or user experience designer it primarily concerns the design of interface elements and layouts, which is mostly a creative design aspect informed by user characteristics; for an industrial product designer it concerns the form of the product, namely its shape, size, and look; and for an electronic engineer it concerns hardware-level features, such as more sensors, smaller chips to reduce size, and a more power-efficient battery.

User-centered design is a design that results from applying a user-centric approach, and it involves users actively or passively in the design or development lifecycle used to build a usable software application.
Ben Shneiderman coined the term user-centered design in 1986 in the context of graphical user interfaces.
The objective of user-centered design is to design products that increase usability.

Cooperative design (coined by Greenbaum and Kyng in 1992), participatory design (Schuler and Namioka, 1993), contextual design (Beyer and Holtzblatt, 1997), and human-centered design (the standard term preferred by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) rather than user-centered design) are related terms that are more or less similar in concept to user-centered design and refer to taking users into the design process.
The user-centered software development approach requires that users be actively or passively involved in the overall software development lifecycle chosen to build a system.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, interaction design and modeling of user input should follow a user-centered design approach so that the user can provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, perceptual design and modeling of output requires a user-centered design approach because it is crucial to ensure that generated output stimuli match the user's perception of them, so that the user can perceive and understand the output easily.

User-centered design, also called user-centric design, human-centric design, or participatory design, is an approach that actively or passively involves users in the overall design lifecycle, including design and implementation, with the objective of designing application software products that are usable.

User-centered design (UCD), also called user-centric or human-centric design, is a design approach in which the design is based on the user's abilities, context, goals, needs, and expectations, and is ideally driven from the users' point of view rather than by the programmer's convenience.

never_defined.name: application software
never_defined.definition: Application software is interactive software that is intended for laypersons and, in a typical VR system, is the highest layer above a game engine.

never_defined.name: deployment
never_defined.definition: Deployment is the development stage in which a built system is made available, either as a native application requiring tailored software development kits or as a web application that allows the experience to be obtained remotely without a specific device.

never_defined.name: client
never_defined.definition: Client is usually separate from end users and is a source of functional and non-functional requirements in interactive system development, and may not accept the system being developed.

never_defined.name: prototyping
never_defined.definition: Prototyping is a stage in the design, prototyping, and evaluation cycle of interactive system development, a cycle repeated with quick evaluation to find problems and refine the design.

never_defined.name: interactive-system design
never_defined.definition: Interactive-system design is a kind of design in which user classes provide a starting point for making decisions and users must be taken into account in every stage and involved as active or passive participants.

never_defined.name: development lifecycle
never_defined.definition: A development lifecycle is a lifecycle used to build a usable software application and to account for users' characteristics, needs, and expectations.

never_defined.name: user-centric software design
never_defined.definition: User-centric software design is the design of usable systems that meet the needs and expectations of laypersons.

never_defined.name: software development
never_defined.definition: Software development is the use of programming to create a prototype, which high-fidelity prototyping can do on a reduced scale.

never_defined.name: extended reality software
never_defined.definition: Extended reality software is software that creates a relationship between a user and a virtual environment.

never_defined.name: interactive software
never_defined.definition: Interactive software is a kind of software, such as extended reality (XR) application software intended for laypersons, that is developed through the interactive system development lifecycle.

never_defined.name: calendar application
never_defined.definition: A calendar application is an application that displays a fixed and large number of elements, such as month names, dates, and possibly the year.

never_defined.name: stage
never_defined.definition: A Stage is a step in an interactive system development lifecycle, a set of stages that should ideally be followed in a particular sequence, with iterations that may return to a previous stage.

never_defined.name: participant
never_defined.definition: A participant is a user selected for an experiment on the basis of a user profile so that the selected users form a representative sample of the whole user group.

never_defined.name: user-centric design approach
never_defined.definition: A user-centric design approach is an approach to usable interactive systems and extended reality software that includes users' needs and expectations, requiring a highly iterative software development lifecycle with loops between stages.

never_defined.name: feasibility study
never_defined.definition: A feasibility study is a stage in the interactive system development lifecycle.

never_defined.name: analysis
never_defined.definition: Analysis is part of the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development and a step in developing a model from empirical data.

never_defined.name: specification
never_defined.definition: Specification is a stage in the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development.

never_defined.name: maintenance
never_defined.definition: Maintenance is part of the iterative software development lifecycle for interactive system development.

never_defined.name: end user
never_defined.definition: End user is involved in interactive system development from the requirement-gathering stage onward, usually distinct from the client, and usability requirements primarily come from the end user.

never_defined.name: requirement analysis
never_defined.definition: Requirement analysis is an analysis in the development of interactive systems that typically refers to the requirements of the client.

never_defined.name: ethnographic study
never_defined.definition: Ethnographic study is one of the methods for gathering end user requirements in the requirement-gathering stage.

never_defined.name: cultural probe
never_defined.definition: A Cultural probe is a method for gathering end user requirements in the requirement-gathering stage.

never_defined.name: turnaround time
never_defined.definition: Turnaround time is the overall project time that increases significantly when repeated design, prototype, evaluation, coding, and testing cycles are not completed quickly, potentially causing cost overruns.

never_defined.name: coding
never_defined.definition: Coding is a stage in interactive system development, carried out after code design and before code testing.

never_defined.name: iterative software development life cycle
never_defined.definition: Iterative software development life cycle is a software development life cycle that has three evaluation points: early evaluation, code testing, and empirical study.

never_defined.name: usability testing
never_defined.definition: Usability testing is a systematic empirical study that involves users to estimate whether an interactive system is usable, distinct from code testing, which only shows that a system is executable.

never_defined.name: iterative design
never_defined.definition: Iterative design is the design of usable extended reality systems in which the design-prototype-evaluate cycle is the only loop designed to be performed quickly, and other loops should not be frequent.

never_defined.name: development cost
never_defined.definition: Development cost is the cost of a project in manpower, time, and resources.

never_defined.name: development stage
never_defined.definition: A development stage is one of the stages in building a usable extended reality system that should be completed carefully to avoid the need to return to previous stages.

never_defined.name: design-prototype-evaluate
never_defined.definition: Design-prototype-evaluate is one of the stages of the interactive system development lifecycle in which building interactive software differs from building regular software.
